1.note: Jeremiah is using the term **behold** to focus his readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and now see this]

A **fig** is a sweet fruit that grows on fig trees. If your readers would not be familiar with what a fig is, you could use the name of a similar fruit that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [baskets of a sweet fruit]

The expression **set** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [were standing to the face of the temple of]

Here, **the face** represents the front. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the front of the temple of Yahweh] or [before the temple of Yahweh]

1.q: אַחֲרֵ֣י הַגְל֣וֹת נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֡ל אֶת־יְכָנְיָ֣הוּ בֶן־יְהוֹיָקִ֣ים מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָה֩ וְ⁠אֶת־שָׂרֵ֨י יְהוּדָ֜ה וְ⁠אֶת־הֶ⁠חָרָ֤שׁ וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠מַּסְגֵּר֙ מִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַ⁠יְבִאֵ֖⁠ם בָּבֶֽל
1.note: Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the first ripe figs** of the season are especially good, so were the figs in this basket. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as good as the figs that ripen earliest in the season]

The expression **could not be eaten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. This also occurs in verses 3 and 8. Alternate translation: [people could not eat]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **badness**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verses 3 and 8. Alternate translation: [because they had spoiled]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4.

Jeremiah is using the term **saying** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Jeremiah is using the term **word of Yahweh** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke to me]

5.q: כַּ⁠תְּאֵנִ֥ים הַ⁠טֹּב֖וֹת הָ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה כֵּֽן־אַכִּ֞יר אֶת־גָּל֣וּת יְהוּדָ֗ה
5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **these good figs** are pleasing to the one who sees them, so the people of Judah whom Yahweh sent into exile are pleasing to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as these good figs are pleasing to anyone who sees them, so I will be pleased with the exile of Judah]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **exile**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the exiled people of Judah]
Jeremiah is using **Thus says Yahweh** to introduce a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

6.note: Here, **my eyes** represents Yahweh’s attention and care. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And I will give them my attention for good]

6.q: וּ⁠בְנִיתִי⁠ם֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א אֶהֱרֹ֔ס וּ⁠נְטַעְתִּ֖י⁠ם וְ⁠לֹ֥א אֶתּֽוֹשׁ
6.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will surely establish them and not destroy them]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Judah were a building that he would **build** up and not **tear** down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause them to prosper and not ruin them]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative words **tear them down** and **uproot them**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and keep them safe, and I will plant them and let them remain there]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Judah were a tree that he would **plant** and not **uproot**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will establish them permanently and not drive them away]

7.note: Yahweh is speaking as if the desire to know him were a **heart** that he could give to the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the inward desire to know me]

The pronoun **I** is stated separately, even though the verb translated as **I will be** already includes this meaning. Yahweh is doing that to emphasize his commitment to being the God of his people. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and I will surely be their God]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah whom Yahweh sent away into exile. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and I, I will be to those exiles from Judah for God]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because they will return to me with all of their heart]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people had traveled away from him and would **return** to him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will become completely devoted to me again]

8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the bad figs** are unfit for anyone to eat, so Zedekiah and those with him are unfit in Yahweh’s sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And just as the bad figs are unfit for anyone to eat because they are spoiled]

The expression **cannot be eaten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that no one can eat]

Jeremiah is using the expression **thus says Yahweh** to indicate that what he is reporting is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remnant**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and those who are left in Jerusalem]

9.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **horror** and **evil**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [to be something horrifying and harmful]

Here, **for** marks **evil** as the goal or purpose of **I will give them to horror**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [And I will give them horror so that evil will happen to them] or [And I will harm them through horror]

Yahweh says **all of the kingdoms of the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [to very many kingdoms of the earth]

The terms **a reproach**, **a proverb**, **a taunt**, and **a curse** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the four terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for an object of utter scorn]

The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where I, Yahweh, will drive the people of Judah there]

10.note: Here, **the sword** represents war. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [warfare]

Here, **fathers** represents ancestors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to the people they descended from]
